# XChem fragment-screening lab: the full scope can't be built for USD 300,000

**Short answer:** I couldn't fit a lab with all the equipment you listed into USD 300,000 using this catalog. The cheapest complete design I could build costs about **USD 704,000**, roughly 2.3× your budget. The budget check against that design failed, so I retract any suggestion that it fits. Below is the full design as a provisional design, followed by what $300k can and can't buy.

## Provisional full-scope design (USD 704,253, catalog estimates)

| Function | Item | USD |
|---|---|---|
| Acoustic soaking | Beckman Echo 525 (the only catalog item that can do crystal soaking) | 246,083 |
| Imager with plate hotel | Formulatrix Rock Imager 182 (one camera, 182 plate slots) | 240,144 |
| Drop setter | Formulatrix NT8 | 70,450 |
| Purification | Cytiva ÄKTA go | 49,590 |
| Expression | Infors Multitron Pro shaker / Eppendorf 5810 R centrifuge / Q700 sonicator | 25,000 / 21,619 / 6,100 |
| Protein QC and concentration | Mini-PROTEAN gel system / NanoDrop | 1,568 / 15,167 |
| Harvesting | Crystal Shifter (price may be a web-shop placeholder) | 13,400 |
| Cryo | LN2 dewar / CX100 dry shipper | 2,049 / 1,398 |
| Benches | Handling bench / vibration-isolation table | 5,530 / 6,155 |

**Not included in that total:** installation, service, consumables, O₂ monitoring and ventilation for the LN2 area, and a temperature-controlled imager option. The Echo and the Rock Imager together cost about USD 486k, which is already well over the budget on their own.

## What USD 300k can buy from this catalog
- **Without the Echo and the Rock Imager**, everything else costs about USD 218k.
- **No catalog imager with a hotel fits in the remaining ~USD 82k.** The bench-top Rock Imager 2 has a placeholder price of USD 50–240k, holds only 2 plates and has no hotel.
- **No cheaper alternative exists in the catalog for soaking:** the Echo 525 is the only item that can do it.

So the most USD 300k realistically covers is expression, purification, drop setting, Shifter harvesting and the cryo equipment. Soaking and imaging would have to be outsourced or done on shared core equipment.

## Assumptions I made (none came from you)
- **Target:** 50 successfully mounted crystals per day.
- **Staff and hours:** 8 h days. The final run used 2 protein scientists and 1 crystallographer.
- **Room and site:** 8 × 6 m room, biosafety level 1, LN2 as the only hazard.
- **Growth:** at 20 °C, for 3 days (could range from 1 to 14 days).
- **Protein:** one expression lot is assumed to make enough protein for one crystallisation plate. This is a placeholder, not a measured yield.
- **Diffraction:** done at an outside synchrotron. Shipping plus the beamline queue is assumed to take 7 days. I did not add an in-house X-ray.
- **Harvesting:** 32 mount attempts per plate.
  - At the Shifter's published average of 35 s per crystal, that is 32 × 35 = **1,120 s (about 19 min) per plate**, with a person present the whole time.
  - The published success rate is 86%, so each plate gives about **27.5 usable crystals**. Failed mounts aren't counted as output.
  - The same paper (Wright et al. 2021) reports about 8 crystals/hour for fully manual work without the Shifter. That survey included other tasks. At that rate the same 32 attempts would take about 4 h.
- **Imaging:**
  - Each inspection takes 3 min per plate, and the imager has one camera.
  - Only the day-0 and final inspections are modelled. Inspections in between are not.
  - Plates grow in the imager's plate storage, which the simulator tracks separately from the camera.
- **Dry shipper:** I assumed 5 min of hands-on time per puck to load it. Its 12.6-day cold hold time is only how long it stays cold, not how long any step takes.
- **Fragment soaking time:** not modelled. How long crystals sit in the fragment solution after the Echo adds it isn't counted anywhere.

## Simulation results (model predictions, not measured)
- **First run (1 protein scientist):** median 33.6 crystals/day.
  - The protein scientist was busy 71% of their shift.
- **Second run (adding a second protein scientist):** median 40.5 crystals/day (10th–90th percentile range 24.4–65.9).
  - Only a 28% chance of reaching the target.
  - Purification time had the biggest effect on throughput. Runs queued for the single ÄKTA for about 17,000 s (4.7 h) on average.
- **Independent check:** a separate check of the same design gave a median of 52.7 crystals/day. That run uses different settings, so I'm reporting both numbers rather than treating 52.7 as confirmation. Treat meeting the target as uncertain either way.
- **Layout:** zero violations. The cryogen and vibration-free zones were placed without problems.
- **Synchrotron turnaround:** about 169 h of the roughly 455 h from expression to analysis. Changing the lab layout can't shorten this.

I stopped after one change. A second ÄKTA would probably be the next useful step, but it would add about USD 50k to a design that is already well over budget.

## Recommendation
- **To get the full scope:** plan for about USD 700–750k plus installation and LN2 safety systems.
- **To stay at USD 300k:** buy the expression, purification, NT8, Shifter and cryo equipment, and get acoustic soaking and plate imaging from a facility. XChem-style user programmes offer this.

All prices and throughput figures here are catalog estimates and model predictions. They are not quotes or measured performance, and nothing in this design is safety-certified.

These are the cheapest catalog options that do each job. All prices are catalog estimates, not quotes:

- **Even the cheapest possible setup is about USD 481,000.** That swaps in the bench-top Rock Imager 2, whose price is only a placeholder (USD 50k–240k). It also holds just **2 plates and has no hotel**, so crystal growth would need separate incubated storage. So it isn't the imager hotel you asked for.
- **The Echo 525 alone is about 82% of your budget.** The Rock Imager 1000 alone (about USD 350k) is more than the whole budget.

So I don't think any design from this catalog can include every item you listed for USD 300,000. I won't trim the scope or drop equipment without asking you.

## Questions before I design

1. **Budget or scope:** Which would you prefer?
   - (a) Raise the budget to roughly USD 650–750k for the full lab.
   - (b) Keep USD 300k and drop or outsource some instruments. Typical options are outsourcing acoustic soaking, using a shared or core imager, or buying protein instead of expressing it.
   - (c) Let me build a provisional design that shows the budget gap clearly.
2. **Throughput target:** A number and unit, e.g. crystals harvested per day or crystallisation plates per day.
3. **Room:** Width × depth in metres, door positions and any keep-out zones. Note that the drop setter, imager and Echo need a vibration-free area.
4. **Operating hours:** Hours per day, and the number of operators and their shift length. Harvesting needs a person present the whole time.
5. **Hazards and site:** I'll assume cryogens (LN2) and an expression/biosafety level of BSL-1 unless you tell me otherwise. Do you have O₂ monitoring and ventilation, and any flammable solvents?
6. **Assumptions to confirm:**
   - Diffraction is done at a synchrotron, with shipping time and the beamline queue modelled as delays. I won't add an in-house X-ray machine.
   - Crystal growth temperature is 4 °C or 20 °C. This decides which Rock Imager cooling version you need.
   - Your expected number of crystals per plate, and your mount success rate. If you don't have these, I'll use the published Shifter figures (about 35 s per crystal, 86% of mounts successful) as the starting assumption.

Once I have these, I'll pick the equipment, run the layout and throughput simulation, check the results, and send you a report.

notes: ASSUMED target: 50 successful (not attempted) crystals/day, 8 h day, 2 operators; user did not supply these.
ASSUMED room 8 x 6 m, single door; vibration-free zone for NT8/Echo/imager; LN2 area needs O2 monitoring and ventilation (not in catalog, not costed).
Diffraction at an external synchrotron; no in-house X-ray.
Growth temperature assumed 20 C (Rock Imager 182 temperature variant not specified in catalog).

equipment.rationale: Shaken flask expression; cheapest catalog cell_culture item.
Cell harvest and clarification; cheaper than Avanti JXN-26 (4x750 mL rotor limits culture volume per spin).
Low-cost lysis.
Requested AKTA; cheapest AKTA in catalog.
Low-cost protein QC (SDS-PAGE).
Protein concentration.
Requested nanolitre drop setter; cheapest in catalog.
Cheapest catalog imager with a hotel (182 slots, 1 camera).
Only catalog item with crystal_soaking capability.
Requested Shifter harvesting.
LN2 storage dewar for filled pucks.
Dry shipper (storage/transit container, ~7 pucks per cane) for synchrotron shipping.
Handling bench for puck-to-shipper loading.
Vibration-free surface for drop setter/Shifter microscope.

# XChem fragment-screening lab: the full scope can't be built for USD 300,000

**Short answer:** I couldn't fit a lab with all the equipment you listed into USD 300,000 using this catalog. The cheapest complete design I could build costs about **USD 704,000**, roughly 2.3× your budget. The budget check against that design failed, so I retract any suggestion that it fits. Below is the full design as a provisional design, followed by what $300k can and can't buy.

## Provisional full-scope design (USD 704,253, catalog estimates)

| Function | Item | USD |
|---|---|---|
| Acoustic soaking | Beckman Echo 525 (the only catalog item that can do crystal soaking) | 246,083 |
| Imager with plate hotel | Formulatrix Rock Imager 182 (one camera, 182 plate slots) | 240,144 |
| Drop setter | Formulatrix NT8 | 70,450 |
| Purification | Cytiva ÄKTA go | 49,590 |
| Expression | Infors Multitron Pro shaker / Eppendorf 5810 R centrifuge / Q700 sonicator | 25,000 / 21,619 / 6,100 |
| Protein QC and concentration | Mini-PROTEAN gel system / NanoDrop | 1,568 / 15,167 |
| Harvesting | Crystal Shifter (price may be a web-shop placeholder) | 13,400 |
| Cryo | LN2 dewar / CX100 dry shipper | 2,049 / 1,398 |
| Benches | Handling bench / vibration-isolation table | 5,530 / 6,155 |

**Not included in that total:** installation, service, consumables, O₂ monitoring and ventilation for the LN2 area, and a temperature-controlled imager option. The Echo and the Rock Imager together cost about USD 486k, which is already well over the budget on their own.

## What USD 300k can buy from this catalog
- **Without the Echo and the Rock Imager**, everything else costs about USD 218k.
- **No catalog imager with a hotel fits in the remaining ~USD 82k.** The bench-top Rock Imager 2 has a placeholder price of USD 50–240k, holds only 2 plates and has no hotel.
- **No cheaper alternative exists in the catalog for soaking:** the Echo 525 is the only item that can do it.

So the most USD 300k realistically covers is expression, purification, drop setting, Shifter harvesting and the cryo equipment. Soaking and imaging would have to be outsourced or done on shared core equipment.

## Assumptions I made (none came from you)
- **Target:** 50 successfully mounted crystals per day.
- **Staff and hours:** 8 h days. The final run used 2 protein scientists and 1 crystallographer.
- **Room and site:** 8 × 6 m room, biosafety level 1, LN2 as the only hazard.
- **Growth:** at 20 °C, for 3 days (could range from 1 to 14 days).
- **Protein:** one expression lot is assumed to make enough protein for one crystallisation plate. This is a placeholder, not a measured yield.
- **Diffraction:** done at an outside synchrotron. Shipping plus the beamline queue is assumed to take 7 days. I did not add an in-house X-ray.
- **Harvesting:** 32 mount attempts per plate.
  - At the Shifter's published average of 35 s per crystal, that is 32 × 35 = **1,120 s (about 19 min) per plate**, with a person present the whole time.
  - The published success rate is 86%, so each plate gives about **27.5 usable crystals**. Failed mounts aren't counted as output.
  - The same paper (Wright et al. 2021) reports about 8 crystals/hour for fully manual work without the Shifter. That survey included other tasks. At that rate the same 32 attempts would take about 4 h.
- **Imaging:**
  - Each inspection takes 3 min per plate, and the imager has one camera.
  - Only the day-0 and final inspections are modelled. Inspections in between are not.
  - Plates grow in the imager's plate storage, which the simulator tracks separately from the camera.
- **Dry shipper:** I assumed 5 min of hands-on time per puck to load it. Its 12.6-day cold hold time is only how long it stays cold, not how long any step takes.
- **Fragment soaking time:** not modelled. How long crystals sit in the fragment solution after the Echo adds it isn't counted anywhere.

## Simulation results (model predictions, not measured)
- **First run (1 protein scientist):** median 33.6 crystals/day.
  - The protein scientist was busy 71% of their shift.
- **Second run (adding a second protein scientist):** median 40.5 crystals/day (10th–90th percentile range 24.4–65.9).
  - Only a 28% chance of reaching the target.
  - Purification time had the biggest effect on throughput. Runs queued for the single ÄKTA for about 17,000 s (4.7 h) on average.
- **Independent check:** a separate check of the same design gave a median of 52.7 crystals/day. That run uses different settings, so I'm reporting both numbers rather than treating 52.7 as confirmation. Treat meeting the target as uncertain either way.
- **Layout:** zero violations. The cryogen and vibration-free zones were placed without problems.
- **Synchrotron turnaround:** about 169 h of the roughly 455 h from expression to analysis. Changing the lab layout can't shorten this.

I stopped after one change. A second ÄKTA would probably be the next useful step, but it would add about USD 50k to a design that is already well over budget.

## Recommendation
- **To get the full scope:** plan for about USD 700–750k plus installation and LN2 safety systems.
- **To stay at USD 300k:** buy the expression, purification, NT8, Shifter and cryo equipment, and get acoustic soaking and plate imaging from a facility. XChem-style user programmes offer this.

All prices and throughput figures here are catalog estimates and model predictions. They are not quotes or measured performance, and nothing in this design is safety-certified.

items.abstract: Despite the tremendous success of X-ray cryo-crystallography in recent decades, the transfer of crystals from the drops in which they are grown to diffractometer sample mounts remains a manual process in almost all laboratories. Here, the Shifter, a motorized, interactive microscope stage that transforms the entire crystal-mounting workflow from a rate-limiting manual activity to a controllable, high-throughput semi-automated process, is described. By combining the visual acuity and fine motor skills of humans with targeted hardware and software automation, it was possible to transform the speed and robustness of crystal mounting. Control software, triggered by the operator, manoeuvres crystallization plates beneath a clear protective cover, allowing the complete removal of film seals and thereby eliminating the tedium of repetitive seal cutting. The software, either upon request or working from an imported list, controls motors to position crystal drops under a hole in the cover for human mounting at a microscope. The software automatically captures experimental annotations for uploading to the user's data repository, removing the need for manual documentation. The Shifter facilitates mounting rates of 100-240 crystals per hour in a more controlled process than manual mounting, which greatly extends the lifetime of the drops and thus allows a dramatic increase in the number of crystals retrievable from any given drop without loss of X-ray diffraction quality. In 2015, the first in a series of three Shifter devices was deployed as part of the XChem fragment-screening facility at Diamond Light Source, where they have since facilitated the mounting of over 120 000 crystals. The Shifter was engineered to have a simple design, providing a device that could be readily commercialized and widely adopted owing to its low cost.
